newsitem.title: USA: U.S. drugstore chains buy power through mergers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. drugstore chains buy power through mergers.

text.p: The U.S. drugstore industry is consolidating, but transactions seen so far probably represent just a small percentage of those that are yet to come.

Industry experts said there are dozens of second and third-tier chains that are ripe to be acquired because they cannot survive drug pricing pressures or afford the costly computer upgrades that are essential in today's world of managed health care.
"The economics of the industry favor size these days. That wasn't necessarily the case five years ago," said Joseph Ronning of Brown Brothers Harriman.
The consolidation trend moved forward Monday as Phar-Mor Inc and ShopKo Inc joined forces to propose the creation of a new holding company in a transaction valued at $1 billion.
Also on Monday, Revco D.S. Inc announced its intention to take over Big B Inc for $15 per share, or $330 million. Revco said it launched a cash tender offer after it was rebuffed by Big B.
The two proposed transactions come just one month after Thrift Drug Inc, a unit of J.C. Penney Co Inc, said it was buying drugstore chain Fay's Inc for $285 million.
The nation's biggest drug stores, which include Revco, Thrift, Rite Aid Corp and Eckerd Corp, are viewed as best poised to thrive in the consolidating industry.
But the future of smaller chains like Genovese Drug Stores Inc, Arbor Drugs Inc and F & M Distributors is not as clear.
"There are still lots of small regional companies and over time, they're going to be eaten up," said Terrence McEvoy of Janney Montgomery Scott.

Just last Friday, Genovese was forced to publicly address the consolidation issue after a Business Week article cited industry speculation that it could be a target of J.C. Penney. The Melville, N.Y.-based chain said it was not holding any merger discussions.
Industry leaders are seeking to grow by acquisitions in order to combat pricing pressures that have accompanied the dominance of managed health care plans.

"If they can get big enough, they can stand up to the third party payors," Ronning said, noting that more than half of the business handled by some big drugstore chains comes from health maintenance organizations, insurance companies and other third parties.

The smaller chains have become obvious targets following the April termination of a $1.8 billion friendly merger agreement between Rite Aid and Revco. The companies cancelled the pact, which would have created an industry giant with more than 4,500 stores, after federal and state regulators contended the union would drive up consumer prices.
Since then, Rite Aid has said it will focus on acquisitions outside of existing markets. In June, it bought 34 Kentucky and Indiana units from Taylor Drug Stores.
"It's a consolidating industry sector, and I think it's going to be down to maybe a dozen players in the end, more or less, (of) a national scope," said Salomon Brothers analyst Jonathan Ziegler.
